Ship It

From a vibe-coded idea to a live site: Docker, GitHub, hosting, hooks and MCP.

1. It Works On My Laptop

The oldest problem in software: your machine has its own operating system, versions and settings. The server has different ones.

Nova: It runs on my laptop. Why is it broken on the server?

A container bundles an app with what it needs to run, so it behaves the same on your laptop, a teammate's laptop and a server.

That is this comic: Docker, Git and GitHub, hosting, then rules, skills, hooks and MCP.

Vex: Five tools, one road: write with an AI, package it, version it, ship it, keep the AI on a leash.

IN SHORT: Your computer and the server are different machines. Packaging, versioning and careful shipping close that gap.

2. The Vibe

Andrej Karpathy named "vibe coding" on 2 February 2025: forget the code exists, accept all, never read the diffs.

Nova: I describe it, accept everything, paste the errors back. It mostly works.

He said it was "not too bad for throwaway weekend projects". Simon Willison draws the line: if you review, test and understand the code, that is AI-assisted programming, not vibe coding.

That is Willison's golden rule for production-quality AI-assisted work.

Vex: My rule: I do not commit what I could not explain to someone else.

AI code can include bugs and invented functions or libraries. The good news: code either runs or it does not, which is a built-in check.

Skill one: read the diff. Skill two: run it. Skill three: ask the AI to explain anything you cannot.

READ THE DIFF

IN SHORT: Vibe coding means accepting AI code without reading it. It is fun for toys, and risky for anything you ship.

3. Boxes: Docker

An image is a read-only template built from a Dockerfile. A container is a running instance of it.

Docka: The image is the recipe. The container is the meal.

Each container gets its own files. When a container is deleted, the files it changed go with it, which is why they feel disposable.

To reach a container from your browser you publish a port: docker run -p 8080:80 maps port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside.

A named volume lives outside any one container. Delete the container and the volume is still there.

Docka: Want the data to survive? Mount a volume.

Careful: docker compose down -v also deletes the named volumes. That is how people lose a database by accident.

MIND THE -V

IN SHORT: An image is the recipe, a container is a running copy. Containers forget everything unless you give them a volume.

4. A Good Dockerfile

Multi-stage builds use several FROM lines and COPY --from=build to carry over only the finished files. The compilers and caches stay behind.

Docka: Build in a big stage, ship from a tiny one.

The result is a smaller, cleaner image with fewer things an attacker could use.

A .dockerignore file keeps node_modules, logs and temp files out of the build context. Builds get faster and the image gets leaner.

Create a user in the Dockerfile and switch with USER. Docker's docs also say to avoid sudo and to avoid flipping USER back and forth.

Vex: If the app does not need root, do not give it root.

Do not pass secrets with ARG: they can end up in the image history. Use RUN --mount=type=secret so the value is only there during the build.

NO SECRETS IN ARG

Nova: My AI wrote the Dockerfile. I read it anyway.

READ IT

IN SHORT: Build big, ship small. Keep junk and secrets out, and do not run as root.

5. Many Boxes: Compose

Docker Compose describes several services in one YAML file and starts them together with docker compose up.

Docka: App, database, cache: one file, one command.

Compose starts services in dependency order. But with plain depends_on it only waits until a container is running, not until it can answer.

Use depends_on with condition: service_healthy, and a healthcheck such as pg_isready for Postgres.

Plug: So give the database a healthcheck, then wait for it to be healthy.

Put the database files on a named volume so a restart does not wipe them.

ONE FILE, MANY BOXES

IN SHORT: Compose runs your app, database and cache together from one file. "Started" is not the same as "ready".

6. Branches: Git and GitHub

Git saves snapshots of your project. Small commits make it easy to find the change that broke things.

Branch: Commit small and often. Then you can undo whatever the AI breaks.

When two branches change the same lines you get a merge conflict. Read both sides, keep what you need, and test again.

Work on a branch, open a pull request, and let a person (or a check) review it before it reaches the main branch.

Add secrets files to .gitignore, and rotate any key that was pushed, even if you delete it later.

Vex: Never commit the .env file. If a key ever lands in Git, treat it as stolen.

Danger zone: force-pushing and hard resets can erase work. Ask the AI to explain a command before you let it run.

BRANCH FIRST

IN SHORT: Git is the undo button for your project. A branch plus a pull request is how changes get safely reviewed.

7. The Robot Butler: Actions

A GitHub Actions workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows. That is continuous integration: checks that run automatically.

Branch: On every push, a runner tests the code and builds the image.

Fast feedback beats a surprise at midnight: a failing test on the pull request is cheaper than a failing site.

GitHub advises setting the default GITHUB_TOKEN permission to read for contents and increasing it per job.

Hook: Give the token read-only access, then raise it only where a job needs it.

Third-party actions are code that runs with your secrets nearby. Pin them to a full-length commit SHA, because a tag can be moved.

Store each secret as its own GitHub secret, never a blob of JSON, and rotate any secret that shows up in a log.

LEAST POWER

IN SHORT: GitHub Actions runs your tests and builds on every push. Give it the least power it needs.

8. Where It Lives: Hosting

Static hosting serves finished files only: HTML, CSS, JavaScript. Cheap, fast and simple, but no server code and no database.

A container platform runs your Docker image for you. A virtual server (VPS) gives you a machine to manage yourself.

Docka: Need a server or a database? Ship the container.

GitHub Pages is static hosting: sites up to 1 GB, a soft limit of 100 GB bandwidth a month, and not for online shops or SaaS.

With Actions: build, upload-pages-artifact, then deploy-pages into the github-pages environment, with pages: write and id-token: write permissions.

Branch: Pages can publish from a branch, or from an Actions workflow.

Rule of thumb: start static. Move to containers when you need a back end, and to a server only when you need full control.

START SMALL

IN SHORT: Static sites, container platforms and servers are three different homes. Pick the lightest one that does the job.

9. Keys to the Castle: Secrets

The same code can run on your laptop, a test server and production with different settings.

Hook: Config goes in environment variables. Secrets go in a vault, not in Git.

Do not paste real keys into AI chats or screenshots. Treat anything pasted as possibly stored somewhere.

Check screenshots before sharing. Tokens hide in terminal windows and browser tabs.

ROTATE IT

IN SHORT: Secrets live in environment variables and secret stores, never in the code, the image or the chat.

10. Teaching the AI: Rules and Skills

In Cursor, project rules live in .cursor/rules as .mdc files. A simple AGENTS.md at the project root also works.

Plug: Rules are standing orders. Skills are how-to guides loaded when needed.

A rule file has frontmatter: alwaysApply, a description, and globs that attach it only when matching files are in play.

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file, stored in .cursor/skills or .agents/skills. It can also bundle scripts, references and assets.

Short, specific, testable instructions beat long essays.

Nova: I wrote down "never touch the database folder" and it listened.

WRITE IT DOWN

IN SHORT: Rules and skills are written instructions your AI reads, so every session starts with your house style.

11. The Gate: Hooks

In Cursor a hooks.json file registers scripts. Project hooks live in .cursor/hooks.json, personal ones in ~/.cursor/hooks.json.

Hook: Halt. Show me that shell command first.

Hooks are spawned processes that talk JSON over standard input and output. They run before or after stages of the agent loop.

beforeShellExecution can allow, deny or ask before a terminal command runs. beforeMCPExecution does the same for MCP tools.

The stop hook can return a follow-up message, so the agent keeps working until the tests pass. There is a loop limit.

Vex: afterFileEdit formats every file the AI touches. stop can send the agent back to fix failing tests.

Use hooks as guardrails: block force-pushes and writes to production, log every action, and run formatters automatically.

GUARDRAILS

IN SHORT: Hooks are small scripts that run at set moments in an AI agent's work. They can watch, block or tidy up.

12. The Adapter: MCP

The Model Context Protocol connects AI applications to external tools, data and workflows.

Plug: I am the adapter. Any AI app can talk to any tool that speaks MCP.

The app (host) runs one client per server. The server offers capabilities, such as GitHub access, a database or a calendar.

Servers offer three kinds of things: tools (actions the model can call), resources (read-only context) and prompts (templates you invoke).

A local server uses command and args. A remote one uses url and headers. The two files are merged.

Docka: Set it up in .cursor/mcp.json for a project, or ~/.cursor/mcp.json for everywhere.

Do not hard-code keys in mcp.json. Cursor supports ${env:NAME} so secrets come from your environment instead.

ENV, NOT TEXT

Good first servers: your repo host, your docs, a read-only database. Add one at a time and watch what each can do.

IN SHORT: MCP is an open standard that lets AI apps plug into tools and data. One protocol, many servers.

13. Trust Issues: MCP Security

This is tool poisoning, a form of indirect prompt injection. OWASP lists it as a key MCP risk.

Gremlin: I hide instructions inside a tool description. The AI reads them and obeys.

Related tricks: a server that changes its tools after you approved it (a "rug pull"), and one tool quietly steering another.

Prefer short-lived tokens. Never share one token across servers. Read what a server can do before you approve it.

Hook: So: least privilege. Narrow scopes, separate credentials per server.

The MCP spec warns against token passthrough: a server must only accept tokens issued for itself, and must not forward yours downstream.

Keep a human in the loop for sensitive actions, and use a beforeMCPExecution hook to log or block risky calls.

TRUST NOTHING

IN SHORT: Treat every MCP tool and every reply as untrusted. Give each server the least access it needs.

14. Putting It Together

Nova: I ask the AI for a feature on a new branch.

Vex: I read the diff, run the tests, and open a pull request.

Actions run the tests and build the Docker image. Only green builds move on.

Hook: My hooks block dangerous commands and log what the agent did.

Deploy from the main branch: Pages for static sites, a container platform when you need a back end.

SHIP IT

IN SHORT: The safe path is simple: AI drafts, you review, Git records, Actions checks, hooks guard, and only then it ships.

15. Ship It

Start today: put the project in Git, add a .gitignore, read every diff, and deploy something small. Add Docker, Actions, hooks and MCP as the project earns them.

SHIP IT

IN SHORT: You do not need all of this on day one. Add one safeguard at a time, starting with reading the diff.
